n: Abraham opens his record in Ur, the home of his ancestors in the land of the Chaldeans (southern Mesopotamia). He realizes he must find a new home — the first step in a life of faith-driven journeys.

f.g: A people of southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq); Ur is called “Ur of the Chaldees” in Genesis 11:28, 31.

n: Abraham describes what he longs for: peace, greater righteousness and knowledge, to be a father of many nations, and the priesthood blessings of the patriarchs. Through seeking and obedience he becomes a rightful heir and High Priest.

f.g: A phrase also used of Melchizedek (Alma 13:18), Abraham’s priesthood leader (D&C 84:14).

n: This priesthood was passed down from Adam — the first father — through the patriarchs to Abraham. Its roots even reach back before the earth was formed.

f.g: The birthright of patriarchal priesthood leadership, passed from father to son.

n: Abraham sought to be appointed to the priesthood in the same way God had appointed his forefathers, with special concern for his future “seed,” or descendants.
Abraham’s own family had abandoned God’s commandments to worship heathen idols, and they refused to listen to him. His faith began in a home that did not share it.

f.g: peoples who did not worship the true God.

n: Abraham names the gods his fathers turned to — Elkenah, Libnah, Mahmackrah, Korash, and the god of Pharaoh. These names are unknown outside this record; some scholars have suggested links to ancient Near Eastern deities.

f.g: Possibly related to the Semitic title ’el qoneh, “God, creator/possessor” (compare Genesis 14:19).

n: These idol worshippers even sacrificed children, and they tried to kill Abraham through the priest of Elkenah, who also served Pharaoh. “Dumb” idols means mute ones that cannot speak or act.

f.g: dumb = unable to speak; lifeless images.

n: Abraham explains that it was customary for Pharaoh’s priest to sacrifice men, women, and children on an altar in Chaldea, showing Egyptian religious influence reaching into Mesopotamia.

f.g: foreign gods, not the God of Israel.

n: The priest offers sacrifices to Pharaoh’s god and to the sun god called Shagreel, following Egyptian ritual.

f.g: Identified in the text as the sun; several ancient cultures worshipped a sun deity.

n: Even a child was sacrificed as a “thank-offering” on the altar at Potiphar’s Hill, at the edge of the plain of Olishem. Abraham gives specific place names, rooting his story in real geography.

f.g: Some scholars have pointed to an ancient inscription naming a place called Ulisum in northern Mesopotamia.
a sacrifice given in gratitude to a god.

n: The priest had killed three young women, royal descendants of Ham, because they refused to worship idols of wood and stone. Their virtue cost them their lives — they are among scripture’s early martyrs.

f.w: gods of wood or of stone

n: The priests seize Abraham to kill him the same way. Abraham refers readers to an illustration at the beginning of his record — Facsimile 1 in the Pearl of Great Price.

f.w: the representation at the commencement of this record
f.g: Facsimile 1, printed at the start of the Book of Abraham.

n: The altar was shaped like a bed frame and stood before the idols. Facsimile 1 depicts such a lion-shaped couch.

f.g: the frame of a bed.

n: Abraham says he has drawn the idols in the opening figures, which the Chaldeans called “Rahleenos,” meaning hieroglyphics — picture-writing.

f.g: Given in the text as the Chaldean word for hieroglyphics; not attested elsewhere.
the picture-based writing system of ancient Egypt.

n: As the priests raise their hands to kill him, Abraham cries to God. The Lord hears, fills him with a vision, and an angel instantly loosens his bonds.
The Lord speaks by name — Jehovah — and promises to deliver Abraham and lead him from his family to a land he does not know. Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah to be the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.w: a strange land which thou knowest not of

n: Jehovah explains that He has come down to judge these idol worshippers and to destroy the man who tried to kill Abraham — whom He calls “my son.”

f.g: A tender title expressing covenant relationship with God.

n: The Lord promises to lead Abraham personally, to put His name upon him — the priesthood of his fathers — and to cover him with divine power.

f.w: to put upon thee my name

n: As with Noah, God will make Abraham the head of a new beginning; through Abraham’s ministry God’s name will be known forever.

f.w: my name shall be known in the earth forever

n: The Lord destroys the altar and idols and strikes down the priest, causing mourning in Chaldea and Pharaoh’s court. Abraham explains that “Pharaoh” is a title meaning king by royal blood.

f.g: An Egyptian royal title (literally “great house”), not a personal name.

n: This king of Egypt descended from Ham, Noah’s son, and through his mother from the Canaanites. Abraham is explaining Egypt’s royal lineage.
From this lineage came the Egyptian people, preserving the Canaanite line in that land.

f.g: Here, descendants of an ancient people of that name; see Moses 7:6-8.

n: Egypt was first discovered by Ham’s daughter, Egyptus, whose name Abraham says means “that which is forbidden” in Chaldean.

f.g: A Greek/Latin-style form of Egypt’s name (Greek Aigyptos).

n: When she found the land it was flooded; she later settled her sons there. Abraham says the “curse” — a restriction on priesthood — continued through this line.

f.g: Perhaps after the Flood, or reflecting the Nile’s yearly flooding of Egypt.

n: Egypt’s first government was set up by Pharaoh, eldest son of Egyptus, following Ham’s patriarchal (father-led) pattern.

f.g: government led by the father or head of the family line.

n: This first Pharaoh was righteous and wise, trying to copy the order of Adam and Noah. Noah blessed him with earthly blessings and wisdom but not with priesthood rights.

f.w: cursed him as pertaining to the Priesthood
f.g: denied him the patriarchal priesthood right. The Church now teaches that all worthy men may receive the priesthood (Official Declaration 2, 1978).

n: Because Pharaoh’s line lacked the priesthood right, later Pharaohs tried to claim it falsely from Noah through Ham. Abraham’s father was drawn into their idolatry.

f.g: gladly, eagerly — they wanted to claim it.

f.w: my father was led away by their idolatry

n: Abraham promises to trace a chronology from himself back to Creation, since he possesses the ancient records.

f.g: to describe or trace out in detail.

n: After the priest’s death, the famine God had foretold for Chaldea comes to pass.
The famine spreads through Chaldea and torments Abraham’s father, Terah, who then repents of trying to kill his son. Hard times soften his heart — at least for a time.

f.g: Terah (Genesis 11:26-32; Abraham 2:5).

n: The Lord preserved the patriarchs’ records in Abraham’s hands, including knowledge of the creation, planets, and stars. Abraham will write some of this for his descendants — setting up chapters 3–5.

f.w: the planets, and of the stars
for the benefit of my posterity
